messages.subject_clean: predictSE.zip and large abundance predictions
messages.body_plain:
I've used the function predictSE.zip to generate predictions of brood abundance at a wetland basin level using ZIP hierarchical models (pcount).  The generated predictions make sense at the wetland basin level, but when I scale them up, say to a level of abundance per square mile given a certain set of wetlands, the predictions seem overly large....could this have anything to do with the Poisson distribution I used?  And is there any way to get the predictions to include predictions of "zero"?  This might scale down the higher level summed abundance values and also would seem more realistic to me as I doubt every wetland is occupied....

Any suggestions are appreciated
Thanks
KC

messages.subject_clean: Advantages of multi-season, multi-species model?
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a query on multi-species models that I’m hoping to gain some insight on. I’m modeling occupancy of two species in PRESENCE and currently have two independent multi-season models, one for each species. To model species interactions, I’ve included the occurrence of one species as both a site and detection variable for the other (and vice versa) and am hoping to elucidate any potential interference competition.  I’m wondering, because I’m only dealing with 2 species, is there any additional ecological insight that could be gained from implementing a multi-season, multi-species model instead of my current approach?

Thanks in advance!

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Advantages of multi-season, multi-species model?
messages.body_plain:
If you are referring to multi-species models that treat species identification as a random effect, unfortunately you won't be able to fit such a model with only 2 species.  As with any random effects model you want a good number of groups (>10) to properly estimate the random effects distribution (also known as the community-level prior distribution in this case).

You could build a model that treats species as a fixed effect for some parameters while others are shared (no difference between species) if you had a reasonable argument for doing so, since this could potentially increase the precision for the shared parameters.  Model selection could help you explore that.

messages.body_plain: Not sure how you are generating your predictions but the lambda from a ZIP model gives you the mean abundance (N) for sites that have the species present. messages.subject: null models and plot level estimates
messages.subject_clean: null models and plot level estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am interesting in getting plot level estimates of bird abundance, that are corrected for imperfect detection. Data are from point count surveys from 56 plots and birds were recorded in 3 distance bands 0 - 50 m, >50 m - 100m, and > 100 m - 150m. I have truncated the data set to the first two distance bands as there are very few detections in the > 100m - 150 m bin. I am working with a dataset that contains multiple species of birds with similar EDRs and singing rates, based on the literature. I am interested in the group values, not individual species values.

Based on my understanding from help files, vignettes, and answers on this forum, I have run models of this form:

mods1$hnp<-distsamp(~1 ~1,umfwellAC1, output = "density", unitsOut = "ha", keyfun = "halfnorm", se = TRUE)
and use bup(ranef(mods1$hnp), type = "mean") to extract the plot level estimates.

I am new to this package and these statistical methods, so my questions (which may be naive) are:

1. Is ranef the correct function to use to get corrected density estimates at the individal plot level.
2. I am only interested in correcting the density estimates based on the detection function estimated from the distance information. Am I correct in thinking that that is what this null model formulation is doing?  I've been reading Royle and Dorazio 2008 to better understand the way the models work, however my concern (based on my imperfect understanding) is that the detection model or the abundance part of the model is using the variation among plots as well as the distance data to make the plot level estimates and thus is smoothing out variability among plots somehow, that I would like to remain unmodelled.

I appreciate any responses from folks who have a better grasp on these models than I!

Thank you in advance!
Kim

Hi Kim,

I think you are worrying that the site abundance estimates are estimates of random effects in a random effects model, and random effects estimates are shrunk. The estimate of one site is affected by the data from all sites due to the structure of the hierarchical model. There is nothing you can do about this (except for fitting a non-hierarchical distance sampling model to the data from each site separately, but then remember the « 60-80 rule » …).

Why are you interested in the plot-level abundance ?

I am currently working on some 15 odd years of nocturnal forest mammal data (from spotlight surveys) using pcountOPEN.  I have 137 sites and 35 primary periods (defined by year/season combinations in which I felt it reasonable to assume closure).  However, I am really interested in differences between two longer time-periods (defined as before and after primary period 20 or so, also coded as "time_step3" in my yearlySiteCovs in my model).  Using the example code from the pcountOPEN documentation I have been able to calculate yearly estimates using ranef() but I would like to do this in a way similar to that acheived using predict(), such that I get predictions across a range of values of MATemp, but averaged over the two groups of primary periods of interest.  Any thoughts on how to do this would be much appreciated.
Cheers
A

[forthcoming workshop on hiearchical modeling will be at Cornell University, August 2012, details below]

August 2014 Workshop on Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology using BUGS and R: site-structured models for abundance

Instructors: Marc Kéry & Andy Royle, Swiss Ornithological Institute & USGS Patuxent Wildlife Research Center
Date: 13–15 August 2014
Venue: Cornell University, Ithaca New York
Computers: Bring your own laptop with latest R/unmarked and WinBUGS/OpenBUGS/JAGS
Course fee: USD$550 (normal rate), USD$350 (student rate).

The analysis of abundance and of the dynamic rates governing their change lies at the core of ecology and its applications such as conservation and wildlife management. Metapopulation designs, where repeated measurements of some quantity such as counts or distance measurements are made at a collection of sites, underlie a vast number of studies in ecology and management. Inference about such data is conveniently based on hierarchical models, where one submodel describes the underlying true state of the process (e.g., abundance at a site) and another submodel describes the observation process that connects the true state to the observations.

In recent years, much progress has been made in the development of methods and computer algorithms to fit hierarchical models. In particular, Bayesian statistical analysis and the general-purpose Bayesian software package WinBUGS have opened up entirely new possibilities for ecologists to conduct complex population analyses. On the other hand, the R package unmarked contains a wealth of functions to analyse hierarchical models of abundance in a frequentist mode of inference.

This course introduces key hierarchical models used in the analysis of abundance and its spatial and temporal patterns, and provides both Bayesian and the frequentist methods for their analysis. We use package unmarked in R as well as WinBUGS and JAGS to fit and understand some of the most widely used models for the analysis of animal and plant populations. These include:
- binomial (Royle 2004) and multinomial N-mixture models (e.g., removal, double-observer) for the analysis of distribution and abundance,
- CAR modeling of spatial autocorrelation in abundance
- hierarchical distance sampling models (e.g., Royle et al. 2004, Conn et al. 2012),
- dynamic models of abundance (Royle & Dorazio 2008; Dail & Madsen 2011)

This is an intermediate-level workshop with about 80% spent lecturing and 20% on solving exercises. A working knowledge of modern regression methods (GLMs, mixed models) and preferentially of program R or another programming language is required. No previous experience with program WinBUGS is assumed (but, of course, it is beneficial).

Please bring your own laptops and install a recent version of R, with the latest version of package unmarked, plus JAGS and/or WinBUGS 1.4., with the upgrade patch and the immortality key decoded (in this order, only for the latter). OpenBUGS should work for most of what we do.

Please apply here by 1 July 2014:

https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1rabj8gKVm37TVnFyKqsi4lR0CMfxL9DDMh3o--GRpKA/viewform

messages.subject_clean: Multiseason model - bugs/jags code and request for feedback
messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

I have been working on this model for my project, and I hope some of you will consent to take a look and provide advice on whether it looks right, and if possible, weigh in on how best to approach model selection. I have a multi-season model for abundance data collected in 1999, 2000, 2005, 2006, 2012, and 2013 (3 sampling rounds per season); there are 6 treatments and 4 dominant tree cover types (this is a forestry experiment) which I expect to interact. I am using informative priors for detection probability estimated for each species by the Boreal Avian Modelling project (http://www.borealbirds.ca/) - in previous models using observation covariates with uninformative priors, my results unrealistically underestimated detection probability and overestimated abundance (4-5x larger than observed abundance).

I have not had luck figuring out a good method for model selection in addition to Bayesian p-values; so far it seems like my best option is WAIC, either calculated manually or using Stan, but as an MSc student I find that I'm floundering when I investigate these methods, although I plan to continue reading about them. I am grateful for any advice more experienced users can offer.

My apologies for posting bugs/jags code in the unmarked forum: my hope is that users familiar with both will be able to lend insights that would be harder to find in your average bugs list. Annotated and truncated code follows for one of my candidate models. This one converges quickly and completely, although my temporal auto-correlation is non-significant (based on the posterior distribution for rho).

Thanks very much,
Sonya Odsen

---

model {

    # Priors

    alpha.year ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    alpha.year2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

    for (i in 1:ntrt){
    omega.trt[i] ~ dunif(0,1)    # zero-inflation according to treatment
    for (j in 1:ntype){
    alpha.int <http://alpha.int>[i,j] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
    }
    }

    # Prior detection probability, on the logit scale
    for (k in 1:nyear){
    beta[k] <- exp(0.6984804)/(1+0.6984804)
    }
    tau.p <- 1/(sd.p*sd.p)
    sd.p ~ dunif(0,10)

    # Temporal auto-regression
    for (k in 1:nyear){
    eps[k] ~ dnorm(0, tau.eps)
    }
    tau.eps<- 1/(sigma.eps*sigma.eps)
    sigma.eps ~ dunif(0,10)
    rho ~ dunif(-1,1)

    # Likelihood

    # Zero-inflation as a function of treatment
    for (i in 1:nsite) {
    z[i] ~ dbern(omega[i])
    omega[i] <- omega.trt[trt[i]]

    # True abundance as function of year and treatment*cover type
    # Data for 1999, 2000, 2005, 2006, 2012, and 2013
    # AR-1 applies only to 2000, 2006, and 2013

    # Year 1
      N[i,1] ~ dpois(lam.eff[i,1])
      lam.eff[i,1] <- z[i]*lambda[i,1] + 0.00000001
      log(lambda[i,1]) <- log.lambda[i,1]
      log.lambda[i,1]<- alpha.year*X[1] + alpha.year2*pow(X[1],2) +
               alpha.int <http://alpha.int>[trt[i], type[i]]

    # Year >1
    for (k in 2:nyear){
      N[i,k] ~ dpois(lam.eff[i,k])
      lam.eff[i,k] <- z[i]*lambda[i,k] + 0.00000001
      log(lambda[i,k]) <- log.lambda[i,k]
      log.lambda[i,k]<- alpha.year*X[k] + alpha.year2*pow(X[k],2) +
               alpha.int <http://alpha.int>[trt[i], type[i]] + corr[k]*rho*eps[k-1]
    }

      # Probability of detection

      for (k in 1:nyear){
        for (j in 1:nrep){
        y[i,j,k] ~ dbin(p[i,j,k], N[i,k])
        p[i,j,k] <- exp(lp[i,j,k])/(1+exp(lp[i,j,k]))
        lp[i,j,k] ~ dnorm(beta[k], tau.p)

    # Truncated: rest of code computes residuals, expected values, and fit for building residual plots
    # and performing posterior predictive check (Bayesian p-value)

        } # j
      } # k
    } # i
 }

Hi Dan,
Thanks for your helpful reply.  I have had a go at doing as you suggested, but in the end decided it was simpler to model the time-step effect by splitting my data into the time-steps and stacking site-time_step combinations (as suggested elsewhere by Andy: "...based on stacking data from multiple years on top of each other and basically treating "year x site" as "effective sites").  This has allowed me to produce some plausible models, e.g.:

> (fm36a <- pcountOpen(~MATemp+MATemp2+ time_step3 +MATemp.time_step3 + MATemp2.time_step3,
+                      ~1, ~1, ~wet+wind+season+temp_anomaly+moon+decimal_start, spp.umf,
+                      K=tk,mixture = "ZIP", dynamics = "constant", se = TRUE))

Call:
pcountOpen(lambdaformula = ~MATemp + MATemp2 + time_step3 + MATemp.time_step3 +
    MATemp2.time_step3, gammaformula = ~1, omegaformula = ~1,
    pformula = ~wet + wind + season + temp_anomaly + moon + decimal_start,
    data = spp.umf, mixture = "ZIP", K = tk, dynamics = "constant",
    se = TRUE)

[1] 17.78615

> max(N.hat0[,17])
[1] 72.39437

Warning message:
In .local(object, ...) :
  Method to compute SE for ZIP model has not been written
